item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
item.description: null On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona. Mariner 9 worked for one year in orbit. When it ran out of gas, NASA shut it off. But the spacecraft remains one of the most famous Mars voyagers of all time. The Mariner 9 spacecraft, seen here in a NASA model, was the first to orbit Mars in 1971. (Image credit: NASA) Here's why it mattered Mariner 9 cemented its place in space history when it entered into orbit around Mars, the first human-built spacecraft ever to do so. The NASA spacecraft actually beat the Soviet Union's own Mars 2 spacecraft to the Red Planet, even though Mars 2 "had an 11-day head start," NASA said in a mission description . (Mars 2 would go on to be the first human-built craft to impact the surface of Mars when it crashed into the Red Planet.) But it was the science from Mariner 9 that transformed Mars from a mysterious Red Planet into a full world for humans to explore. The Boldest Mars Missions in History The Mariner 9 mission first saw the peak of Olympus Mons on Mars in the midst of a global dust storm in 1971. (Image credit: NASA/JPL) Mariner 9 carried four primary instruments to study Mars, including a camera system for imaging, an ultraviolet spectrometer, an infrared spectrometer and an infrared radiometer. The probe mapped 85% of Mars with those tools during its nearly one-year mission. The Mariner 9 spacecraft discovered 20 giant volcanoes on Mars (including Olympus Mars) and made key observations to map Valles Marineris, which runs 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) long acros the Tharsis region and is 120 miles (200 km) wide. "The canyon was named in honor of Mariner 9," NASA said in an overview . In all, Mariner 9 took 7,329 photos of the surface of Mars, mapping the planet down to a resolution of between 1/2-1 mile (1-2 km). It also snapped at least 80 photos of Phobos and Deimos, the two small moons of Mars. By February 1972, Mariner 9's supply of gaseous nitrogen, which it used to feed its attitide control thrusters, had run dry. NASA finally shut down the mission in October 1972. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
item.description: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. Read full article Comments

item.title: Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer
item.description: US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer. Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models." "This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," said DePue in a social media post . "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model." It doesn't sound that insane. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed from revelations that he had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who, in 2023, founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International. That company is reportedly under investigation by US authorities for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China. Huang's departure coincides with a renewed push to tighten US chip export controls. House Speaker Mike Johnson supports the idea . And there are at least four bills awaiting consideration that aim to limit China's access to leading edge AI tech: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, Match Act, and the Cloud Security Act. On Monday, US Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) cited Jensen Huang's "relationship with a suspected Chinese spy" as a justification for passing the AI Overwatch Act, which would codify the Trump administration's existing chip export controls. The Trump administration on Thursday said it's not sure whether Alice Huang was a spy, an allegation denied by Beijing and currently under investigation by the FBI. Whatever the case, the current rules clearly are not working. Only a few weeks ago, Lava, an Israel-based security company, said it had found "32 Nvidia B300 GPUs, part of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra generation, through publicly exposed monitoring endpoints with IP addresses geolocated to China." These GPUs, Lava noted, are subject to US export controls [PDF]. The security biz said its findings followed from the exposure of monitoring systems intended for internal infrastructure management that were publicly exposed. How DePue reached his conclusion The analysis published through DePue's consultancy, "Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs," takes a different approach: analyzing the published weights of various models from Chinese AI labs. item.title: 60 years ago the Leonid meteor shower produced 144,000 meteors per hour. Could it happen again?
item.description: null This year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago , one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come? The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed. In more recent years, most notably 1999 , 2001 and 2002 , lesser Leonid displays of up to "only" a few thousand meteors per hour took place. Unfortunately, that's not likely to be the case this year. In fact, comparatively speaking, this is going to be a lean year for the Leonids chiefly because of the expected lack of any significant activity. Although the Leonids are one of the most famous of all the annual meteor displays, this year they're not likely to be very productive. It's probable they are going to be rather weak and there probably will be long stretches when not a single Leonid will be seen. I'll explain why in a moment. First, let's find out about this shower's lineage. What causes the Leonids? The Leonids are so named because the shower's radiant point, from where the meteors seem to fan out, is located within the constellation of Leo the Lion, from the backward question mark pattern of stars known as " The Sickle." The meteors are caused by the Tempel-Tuttle comet , which sweeps through the inner solar system every 33⅓ years. Each time the comet passes closest to the sun it leaves a "river of rubble" in its wake: a dense trail of dusty debris. A meteor storm becomes possible if the Earth were to score a direct hit on a fresh dust trail ejected by the comet over the past several centuries. The "lion's share" (no pun intended) of comet dust can be found just ahead and trailing behind Tempel-Tuttle. That comet last swept through the inner solar system in 1998. That's why spectacular meteor showers were seen in 1999, 2001 and 2002, with declining numbers thereafter. The most famous depiction of the 1833 Leonids, actually produced in 1888 for the Adventist book Bible Readings for the Home Circle . The engraving is by Adolf Vollmy based upon an original painting by the Swiss artist Karl Jauslin, that is in turn based on a first-person account of the 1833 storm by a minister, Joseph Harvey Waggoner on his way from Florida to New Orleans. (Image credit: Adolf Vollmy - Bible Readings for the Home Circle. Public Domain) When is the best time to look for Leonids? item.title: This year’s bug count just passed 100K
item.description: Chalk up a new record for vulns. The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI. “It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register . “The thing that almost scares the bejesus out of me is while 100K sounds like a lot, in a couple years we're going to say, remember when it was only 100K?” As of the time of our interview, about 4 pm UTC on Friday, VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs, he said. Microsoft alone added 1,094 security flaws to the total count on Tuesday, following 1,474 vulnerabilities the month before. “There's no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we're seeing.” All the major CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) - these are the organizations authorized by the CVE program to assign unique identifiers to security vulnerabilities - like VulnCheck, Microsoft, Oracle, GitHub, and other large enterprise IT vendors “are just screaming into the atmosphere right now,” Bressers said. “It’s AI.” Meanwhile, the percentage of these bugs that are exploited in the wild remains relatively consistent. About 1.4 percent (1,363) of the CVEs published this year have been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. “But obviously, as the number of CVEs grows, [1 percent] of 1,000 is a lot different than [1 percent] of 100,000,” Bressers said. Plus, as other security researchers have documented, the window between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits – often by reverse engineering the patch while end users are still applying the fix – is rapidly shrinking. This is also thanks to AI . From CVE to KEV From January to June, 88 percent of the exploitation observed by CrowdStrike using public proof-of-concept (PoC) code occurred within 48 hours of the code's release. The security firm said China-linked groups such as Vault Panda and Genesis Panda moved even faster, launching attacks within 24 hours of disclosure. Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026. This window has closed even further during the second half of the year, which also seems to coincide with the AI-induced vulnpocalypse . “It’s often just hours,” Bressers said, noting 14 make-me-root vulnerabilities that VulnCheck disclosed on Friday in Copeland refrigeration controllers. Two are under active exploitation. These are the devices that Iranian hackers abused to spoil food and spark fires in supermarkets across Europe . “We published those CVEs, and literally minutes later, we were seeing hits on our honey pots,” Bressers said about the Copeland device vulnerabilities. “We’ve hit a point where with anything that looks interesting, someone is taking that information a

item.title: Meatbags suck at spotting lying LLMs, so let AI narc on itself
item.description: The internet is full of schlock, from biased news and dubious hot takes to false factoids. LogicLens aims to separate fact from fiction using the very same technology behind some of that slop: AI. It’s a simple premise, really: LogicLens, which lives in Chrome as a browser extension , or on iOS in the form of a mobile app called Receipts , combs through articles, social media posts, and other content to check it not only for factual inaccuracies, but also for bad reasoning. LogicLens and Receipts claim to identify logical fallacies , flag reports that misrepresent information, detect content that attempts to polarize an issue, and the like. It also cites sources, so if, for example, you need to call someone out on their BS, you’ll have ammunition. Or, if you’re trying to fact-check something before sharing it, you can get a more accurate view of the situation, and maybe post something else instead. Using the Chrome extension is as simple as clicking on its icon in the list of extensions in the browser. On iOS, the Receipts app is found as a share option. Once it starts, LogicLens scans an article, post, video, etc. to find potential issues of factual or logical inconsistency and flags them for review. If the facts of the matter turn out to contradict your worldview, LogicLens’ creators say they’re not trying to be partisan - you may just not be as informed as you need to be, which hopefully their tool will assist with. “We're not trying to be the referee of truth,” the company’s about page states. “Instead, LogicLens helps uncover the context, so you can decide for yourself without the spin." Of course, AI is increasingly used for online analysis and content review, and LogicLens is no exception. LogicLens doesn't identify the AI models powering its service in its publicly available documentation, but AI is definitely the backbone of the system. According to LogicLens, it's using an AI system that's “Research-backed and custom designed to outperform general models like ChatGPT & even trained experts.” We’ll leave that up to anyone willing to give the tool a spin to decide, but one thing’s for certain: The world needs something. Large language models and image generation tools are increasingly being used to generate internet content slop, and not all of it is as harmless as poorly made commercials for drop-shipped garbage: Some of it is being used to craft very convincing misinformation. A 2024 study found that AI-generated misinformation was even more convincing than stuff crafted by humans - and that was two years ago. Just think how much worse it’s likely become since then. To make matters worse, concerns have been raised about critical thinking skills being on the decline , potentially making it harder for people to identify falsehoods on the internet. item.title: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
item.description: Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time. Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured. Accidental savanna Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country's four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006). item.title: 'Arrival' at 10: Denis Villeneuve's alien visitation classic that reminded us it's good to talk
item.description:
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor. 

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.  

In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In " Star Trek ", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication. But in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun. The film's journey to the big screen began when a screenwriter best known for his work on horror franchises such as "Final Destination", "A Nightmare on Elm Street" and "The Thing" read a short story in an online magazine. Eric Heisserer was so impressed by Ted Chiang's "Understand" that he bought himself a collection of the author's short stories. One in particular, the Nebula Award-winning "Story of Your Life", piqued his interest. "It had a very profound emotional effect on me," he reminisced to Deadline . "I was in tears, and I was both heartbroken and uplifted. My head was just full of big ideas. I had to walk around the block a couple of times afterward and just hug my friends. The next day, I was like, 'Oh god, I want to give this to other people.'" So when 21 Laps (the production company that later went on to make " Stranger Things ") invited Heisserer to discuss possible future projects, the writer mentioned "Story of Your Life". The producers were also smitten. (Image credit: Paramount Pictures) "I was so excited, but I had that dread that a lot of producers get, which is, 'Are the rights available?'" 21 Laps' Dan Levine told the Hollywood Gold podcast. "You read something that blows you away, and then you find there aren't the rights, and there's no chance, you have to move on. So we were trying to track down this Ted Chiang, and he had no agent. He had a day job. He was impossible to find, so we started the hunt for Ted Chiang." An up-and-coming Canadian director named Denis Villeneuve h

item.title: 100 launches! Rocket Lab sends Earth-observing satellite to orbit on milestone mission (photos)
item.description: null Rocket Lab just hit the century mark. An Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite lifted off from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site on Saturday (Nov. 14) at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local New Zealand time). The mission, which Rocket Lab called "The Mountain God Rises," was a big one: It marked the 100th launch to date for the California-based company. The first stage of Rocket Lab's Electron rocket falls back to Earth during "The Mountain God Rises" mission on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) Rocket Lab launched for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-new Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand. That effort failed, but Electron bounced back on its second-ever liftoff, delivering several cubesats to low Earth orbit (LEO) in January 2018. In the years since, the 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron has become one of the most prolific and reliable rockets in the world, carrying small payloads to the final frontier for a variety of customers. And it hit the century mark on Saturday in record-breaking fashion: No commercially developed rocket has gotten there faster, not even SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 , according to Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck. "It's an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket, and a threshold rarely crossed in modern spaceflight," Beck said on Monday (Nov. 9), during Rocket Lab's third-quarter earnings call with investors. "But what matters most to us and our customers is that we have achieved a 96% reliability rate across 99 launches." Electron met the moment in style on Saturday morning, thanks to some fancy livery. "Black rocket 🤝 Golden milestone. Electron is all dressed up for launch 100," Rocket Lab said via X on Tuesday (Nov. 10), in a post that shared a photo of the specially painted first stage. Not all of Rocket Lab's missions have gone orbital, it should be noted: A suborbital variant of Electron known as HASTE , which customers use to test technologies in a hypersonic flight environment, has nine missions under its belt to date. The Electron rocket that flew Rocket Lab's 100th mission sported some special livery. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) "The Mountain God Rises" was Rocket Lab's 11th launch to date for the Tokyo-based company iQPS, which is building a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO. And all went to plan on the mission: Electron's upper "kick stage" deployed a single iQPS spacecraft 357 miles (575 kilometers) above Earth. SAR satellites can see through cloud cover and image our planet at night as well as during the day, offering key advantages over spacecraft that are optimized to view in optical wavelengths. Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:40 a.m. ET on Nov. 14 with news of successful liftoff, then again at 1:30 a.m. ET with news of satellite deployment.

item.title: California's brand-new Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today
item.description: null LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13). After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour , sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall. "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour. The space shuttle Endeavour. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future) "There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience." Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the new wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life. The new Endeavour exhibit features a replica launch tower, from which you can look down at the shuttle. (Image credit: Future) There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with. As for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. And you can see the shuttle from underneath all the way to the top. A replica of the space shuttle Endeavour's flight deck. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future) You can lie on the floor underneath the shuttle's engines, for example, and then take an elevator up the launch tower to come face-to-face with Endeavour's nose. There's even a transparent floor at the top that allows you to stand above the shuttle (though if you have a fear of heights, this might not be for you). This is the abbreviated description, but know that if you are visiting the California Science Center, you will want to budget a serious amount of time to explore all that this new center has to offer. item.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
item.description: null Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up. But every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes. What's happening and when to look You can easily see the Pleiades as a bright misty patch in your peripheral vision during winter. (Image credit: Haitong Yu via Getty Images) The Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns. In mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. Nearby you'll also find orange Aldebaran and the much broader V-shaped Hyades cluster. The Hyades are closer to the sun , but their stars are about 625 million years old. The name "Seven Sisters" creates an immediate observational trap: people assume they're supposed to see seven stars. That's not necessarily true. In fact, six is a common naked-eye result under decently dark conditions (note that the shape of the six brightest is like a mini Big Dipper /Plough), while people with sharp eyesight under darker skies may see more. The cluster itself contains about 1,000 stars. The number you personally distinguish depends on eyesight, sky brightness, atmospheric conditions and how well your eyes have adapted to darkness. That makes M45 much more interesting to me than a simple tick-box target. So tonight, don't just find the Pleiades — count them. How and when I'm watching it Counting the stars you can see in the Pleiades is a fun way to test your naked-eye observing skills. item.title: Nigerian-Born Shirley Emehelu Makes History as New Jersey’s First Immigrant Lieutenant Governor
item.description: Shirley U. Emehelu, New Jersey’s fifth Lieutenant Governor and Secretary of State. Photo Credit: Official Site of New Jersey A Nigerian-born legal leader has made history in New Jersey. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill has officially appointed Nigerian-American Shirley U . Emehelu as the state’s fifth Lieutenant Governor and Secretary of State . Sworn in at the New Jersey Statehouse in Trenton on 9 November 2026, Emehelu has made double history in the process—becoming New Jersey’s first immigrant Lieutenant Governor and forming part of the state’s first all-women Governor–Lieutenant Governor team. Born in Nigeria before moving to the United States at the age of three, Emehelu brings an extraordinary record of public service and legal excellence to New Jersey’s second-highest executive office. Before this historic appointment, she served as Acting State Comptroller , leading key efforts to combat fraud, waste, and abuse while protecting taxpayer funds and strengthening government accountability, and also stepped in as Acting Secretary of State to oversee New Jersey’s elections. Her public sector résumé also includes a two-year tenure as Executive Assistant Attorney General of New Jersey, where she served as the third-ranking official in the New Jersey Attorney General’s Office. In that role, she directly counselled the Attorney General, coordinated oversight for more than 500 attorneys within the Division of Law—New Jersey’s largest legal office—and directed civil defence and enforcement matters across civil rights, environmental protection, labour and consumer protections, data privacy, and firearms safety. New Jersey Lieutenant Governor Shirley U. Emehelu, part of the state’s first all-women Governor–Lieutenant Governor team. Photo Credit: Shirley U. item.title: 'Martian Isolation' is an upcoming sci-fi survival horror game that looks like 'The Martian' and 'Event Horizon' had a horrific child
item.description: null "Martian Isolation" is an upcoming single-player, first-person survival horror game that's just been revealed with a suitably creepy launch trailer. And yes, it does look an awful lot like " The Martian ," doesn't it? There's a lot of survival gameplay on display here that mirrors Mark Watney's tale of survival on the Red Planet, as your stranded protagonist is forced to explore the Martian surface to acquire resources, grow plants, and repair their base. That comparison to Andy Weir's sci-fi masterpiece does fall away as you get further into the trailer, though, when the horror part of the game's description comes into play: Flickering lights, creepy figures stalking the halls of your Martian habitat, and blood dripping from the walls. Oh yeah, that's some good creepy sci-fi horror right there. It's giving " Event Horizon ", and that's always getting a thumbs-up from me. There's no release date scheduled at this time, with the 'Martian Isolation' Steam page simply listing it as "coming soon," though the YouTube trailer description does say it "will be available on Steam in 2027". You can't pre-order yet, but if this looks like your jam, you can add it to your wishlist. Beyond that, we know shockingly little about this title. It's the debut game from Golden Milestone Studio, but there's very little information out there beyond a name. The latest blog post on the game's Steam page says that they're a "small team," but what we've seen so far is encouraging. There seems to be a pronounced split between the survival and horror elements of the game along the day/night cycle. Daytime sees you exploring the Martian surface, smashing rocks, cleaning solar panels, and doing sick jumps on a quad bike. The psychological torment only begins once the sun goes down (they mostly come out at night … mostly), as your character starts encountering cosmic horrors and weird naked zombie men. Mars rover, nice. Golden Milestone Studio Spacesuits, check. Golden Milestone Studio Crafting, of course. Golden Milestone Studio OH SWEET JESUS! Get it away, get it away. Golden Milestone Studio OK, we're good. Mining, cool. Golden Milestone Studio Riding a quad bike on Mars, yes please. Golden Milestone Studio Growing potatoes on Mars, just like that guy in the movie. Golden Milestone Studio Opening a box with power tools, seems excessive but sure. Golden Milestone Studio NOPE! Nope, nope, nope, I'm out! Golden Milestone Studio Are they hallucinations, or is there some malevolent presence hiding in the blood-red sands of Mars ? I'm always looking for new ways to shatter my psyche and possibly soil my pants, so I'll be keeping a close eye on this one. In the meantime, I do need to get back and finish " Routine ." I left my character hiding under a desk months ago, and I haven't been brave enough to go back. As Mama always said, you can't have any Martian horror until you finish your lunar horror first.

item.title: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away
item.description: How do you think you're going to die? If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident." In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. Read full article Comments

item.title: Astronomers trace mystery radio signals back to cosmic odd couple of white dwarf and sun-like star
item.description: null Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star. The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153. GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021. Several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and a companion star, but it has been unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. That means the discovery of GPM J071507−114153 and finding that the pulses come from close to the white dwarf could be a significant step toward understanding the nature of LPTs. The unusual system consists of a small and highly energetic white dwarf pulsar, orbiting a much larger star similar to our sun. (Image credit: ICRAR) "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," team leader and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), Sam McSweeney, said in a statement . "So we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself." The pulses seen by the team also allowed them to detect stellar flares erupting on the sun-like star. "As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence,' which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface," team member Natasha Hurley-Walker of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR), Curtin University, Australia, said. "It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away." South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope. (Image credit: South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO)) Hurley-Walker and the team at ICRAR have been at the cutting edge of rare star systems like this. "We detected this system in a large survey using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia," Hurley-Walker said. "We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position." After the radio telescopes detected this LPT, it was confirmed using the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The visible light follow-up of Keck also confirmed that the star in GPM J071507−114153 was a G-type star, just like the sun. MeerKAT and the MWA are both precursors for the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the world’s largest and most

item.title: Mozilla leaves Solo website owners to go it alone as hosting shuts down
item.description: Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30. Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. S ome 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names. Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ , users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com , with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of. It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will. Mozilla told The Register : "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider." It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere. Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now. Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

item.title: Email addresses used in European school bomb hoaxes spotted in old infostealer logs
item.description: Two email addresses used to send bomb threats that disrupted thousands of Italian schools this week were found exposed in infostealer logs for over a year, experts say. Researchers at Hudson Rock looked into the two university email addresses used to send the bomb threats. One, from Egypt’s Kafrelsheikh University, was scooped up by Vidar – a cybercrime tool that steals saved account credentials and passwords from an infected computer and leaks them to attackers – as far back as October 2021. The other, from Taiwan's Dayeh University, was found among the 284 million addresses included in the massive AlienTXTBASE infostealer dump , dated February 2025. The experts said that the two addresses in infostealer logs do not strictly mean that those behind the bomb threats gained access to the accounts using the previous infostealer compromise. However, it suggests that there was ample time for the universities and Microsoft, which both universities used for authentication, to take action against the accounts that they should have been aware were appearing in infostealer logs. Modern threat intelligence has made infostealer logs highly visible. "Both findings place credential exposure well before the disruption, creating a substantial window in which exposed access could have been investigated and secured," Hudson Rock said . The researchers said that they would need access to details such as the email headers, and data from email providers, including sign-in events and audit records, that could show them more about who sent the email and from what session. Understanding whether the sender authenticated into the account could rule out spoofing, but would not in itself provide proof that the sender used a corresponding password taken from an infostealer log, Hudson Rock noted. There are many ways to get around password-based authentication . The researchers said that in any case where a credential is detected among infostealer logs, the organizations responsible for those accounts must contain them, revoke their access, rotate secrets, and go looking for suspicious activity. "The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft," the researchers said. "An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources." The threats Around 6,300 of Italy's 7,476 state schools received fake bomb threat emails between November 11-12, although only around 390 of them evacuated their respective buildings. The emails contained messaging such as "we will annihilate you," and "we will carry out genocide against Italians," and mention of a "powerful explosive device… with a remote trigger." Early reports suggested that the emails came from a Taiwanese email address and were signed by a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan" – a fictitious state or region roughly mapping to "the land of Misogyny," with "vilayat" meaning

item.title: FutureBit’s Apollo III Bitcoin Miner Hits Micro Center Shelves in Its First Brick-and-Mortar Launch
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine FutureBit’s Apollo III Bitcoin Miner Hits Micro Center Shelves in Its First Brick-and-Mortar Launch FutureBit is putting its Apollo III Full Node on sale Friday at four Micro Center stores, the first time customers can walk into a shop and take home one of the Brooklyn company’s bitcoin miners. The compact home miner, which also runs a full bitcoin node, will be sold in Brooklyn, Miami, Tustin, California, and Austin, Texas, as those stores open Friday, FutureBit said in a release. The four-store launch coincides with the grand opening of Micro Center’s new Austin store, the chain’s 31st U.S. location and its third in Texas. Customers will also be able to reserve a unit online for in-store pickup, the company said. It did not say how many units each store has in stock, or what Micro Center is charging for them. Until now, buyers in North America had to order the machine from FutureBit’s website, where the company says units are in stock and ship in two to three days. Putting it on a computer-store shelf lets a customer look at the hardware, ask how it works and carry it out the same day. “When we started FutureBit, we made weekly trips to the DIY electronics section at the Brooklyn Micro Center to buy parts,” said John Stefanopoulos, founder of FutureBit. “On Friday, someone can walk into that same store, ask how Bitcoin mining works and take home a miner we designed just down the street. We couldn’t be more excited to work with Micro Center on our first physical store launch.” A 6-inch miner that also runs a full node FutureBit’s own shop lists the Apollo III Full Node at $1,099.99 without a storage drive, $1,299.99 with 1 terabyte of SSD storage and $1,399.99 with 2 terabytes. A cheaper, miner-only “Standard” model starts at $899.99 but does not include the full node. The Full Node is rated at up to 18 terahashes per second in Turbo mode, at about 325 watts. In Eco mode, it is listed at about 12 TH/s and 150 watts, with noise under 35 decibels. A Super Eco mode is listed at about 8 TH/s and 80 watts. Power can be adjusted from 50 to 400 watts, and Turbo mode is much louder, at about 55 decibels. Those power figures are measured at the board and can vary by 10%, the product page says. The unit is a 6.5-by-6.5-by-6-inch cube that weighs 6.5 pounds, comes with a one-year limited warranty and is assembled in the United States. It uses new 3-nanometer, American-designed chips, a custom controller and 8 GB of memory, and it includes a built-in solo mining pool. Buyers can also point the miner at a standard bitcoin mining pool. FutureBit says the full node and solo-mining features require an SSD, which is not included in the $1,099.99 configuration. Home mining is not a profit play Bitcoin Magazine covered the Apollo III’s debut in February, when FutureBit introduced the hardware as a way for individuals to run both a miner and a node at home. item.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
item.description: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates. Read full article Comments

item.title: HPE debuts hybrid storage configs: Rising SSD costs hit supercomputing
item.description: HPE is pitching high performance compute customers with hybrid configurations of its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems built for faster throughput, along with a Rack Management Controller that monitors cooling systems. The hardware giant already supplies its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 in all-flash, all-disk, tiered and hybrid configurations, but - we're told - the latest combination offers up to 41 percent more data throughput per storage rack. The E2000 line embeds the Lustre open-source parallel file system, and is generally intended to fit NVMe Gen 5 solid-state drive (SSD) building blocks. For the refreshed hybrid configurations, HPE is combining SSDs with new 32 TB SAS-4 (24 Gb/s SAS) HDDs and new enclosures supporting 74 or 100 drives. HPE says it'll deliver up to 116 GB/s of read throughput and 92 GB/s of write throughput per rack, with up to 32 percent more usable storage capacity per rack for expansion to support the growing size of datasets in HPC, especially where sites are mixing AI and traditional simulation-style workloads. One of the reasons behind these new hybrid configurations could be the ballooning cost of storage, caused by the relentless demand for AI infrastructure skewing the price of components such as memory and many other things. But prices for silicon-based NAND flash SSDs are growing faster than those of good old hard drives , as our colleagues at Blocks & Files reported. HPE says that as demand for data-intensive workloads grows, prices for large SSDs have soared. The company claims the new hybrid configurations let research institutions and national laboratories spend less on storage and put that money toward compute node purchases, without giving up on the performance they need. “When making long-term investments in environments where advanced workloads are rapidly evolving, our customers want scalable, dense, and flexible systems to help them address dynamic shifts in requirements," said Trish Damkroger, HPE senior veep for HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions. The latest hybrid configurations are expected to go on sale in early 2027. HPE's other introduction is a Rack Management Controller, providing what HPE calls "intelligent liquid cooling” via real-time monitoring, leak detection and automated control features. It integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software to gather telemetry and provide control. Several platform-specific versions will be offered, each tailored to different rack-scale systems. Support will launch with HPE's own Cray Supercomputing GX5000 infrastructure, naturally, with versions for Nvidia’s NVL72 and AMD’s Helion and Helios kit to follow. The Rack Management Controller will be available for HPE’s kit in March 2027, with support for AMD and Nvidia expected to follow in June. ®

item.title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
item.description: NASA astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. captured this image of the area surrounding the Red Sea and Nile river valley on November 14, 1966, during their four-day mission in space. Gemini XII was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini Program. NASA Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII , the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program. In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of a different field of exploration, observing Earth from space. The photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface. Their images helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program. One of strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, the director of the United States Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971. In a 1969 statement, Pecora noted that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite (EROS) program he championed, and which later paved the way for Landsat , was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.” For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have provided invaluable data used around the world to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health, land use, and countless other changes to our planet. item.title: Netflix’s ‘Ray Gunn’ gets 2nd trailer, and we're hyped for this animated sci-fi noir from ‘Incredibles’ director Brad Bird
item.description: null Dreaming of a bright and shiny future filled with personal jet packs, levitating autos, and automated gadgets straight out of " The Jetsons ?" Add in a gritty mystery, a notorious private eye, double-crossing aliens, and a bombshell diva framed for a killing, and you’ve got the perfect recipe for "Ray Gunn." Oscar-winning director Brad Bird ("The Incredibles," "Ratatouille") returns to our screens with his new big-budget animated sci-fi project, " Ray Gunn ," and this latest trailer has us primed. "In Metropia, a gigantic city in an alternate future as seen from 1939, private eye Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell) is drawn into a case involving aliens, murder, and a multimedia starlet named Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson)," states the official synopsis. Netflix Films and Skydance Animation's "Ray Gunn" is a stylistic pastiche of classic film noir tropes populated by down-and-out detectives and femme fatales living in the inspiring air of technological optimism viewed through a pre-war America lens. Think "The Fifth Element" meets "Who Framed Roger Rabbit?" and "The Maltese Falcon," and you’re going to be close to this sci-fi whodunnit's vibe, which is intended for more mature audiences and rated PG. "The Incredibles'" Brad Bird serves up a sci-fi detective tale in "Ray Gunn" (Image credit: Netflix) This energetic new preview is locked and loaded with dazzling visuals by Cinesite, freaky creatures, streamlined flying cars, and a blistering pace. And if you listen very closely, The B-52s' "Planet Claire" can be heard playing in the background, which is one of the touchstones that inspired Bird to begin his 36-year journey to bring "Ray Gunn" to life. Was it worth the wait? We'll have to find out. Also starring the vocal talents of Tom Waits, Bobby Cannavale, Alan Tudyk, Matt Berry, and Michelle Rodriguez, "Ray Gunn" opens in select theaters and 70mm screenings Dec. 4. After that, it lands on Netflix on Dec. 18... a date you might want to circle on your calendar, as that’s also the release slot for " Avengers: Doomsday " and " Dune: Part 3. " It's going to be a busy day for sci-fi fans. "Strap in, buster!" Watch Ray Gunn on Netflix on Dec 18: Standard with ads: $8.99/month Standard: $19.99/month Premium (4K): $26.99/month

item.title: Microsoft outage gives customers a crash course in dependence on Redmond
item.description: Microsoft 365 services are slowly recovering from a prolonged outage that has handed critics of single-vendor dependence a particularly unwelcome case study. Ever wondered what it would be like if your IT supplier abruptly pulled the plug? Perhaps the result of a mood swing by an unpredictable political leader? For affected Microsoft customers, the disruption has offered an unwelcome preview. Email? Gone. Messaging with Teams? Iffy. Collaboration? Nope. The list of problems in what Microsoft delicately called a "Service Degradation" is breathtaking. The company put the incident's start at 1826 GMT on November 12. Exchange Online fell over. Viewing recently used files in the Microsoft 365 application was problematic. Copilot threw a wobbly. Microsoft 365 Education was affected (unfortunate, considering the changes the company has made ), and so on. At 1401 GMT on November 13, Microsoft reported: "We're continuing to see improvements in service availability," but the damage has surely been done. If the outage halted work at your organization, then questions will have to be asked. Even Microsoft's rivals had some sympathy for the engineers and administrators dealing with the problems. Jos Poortvliet, co-founder of Nextcloud, told The Register : "Mistakes happen in the IT industry. This holds true for companies of all sizes, including us. Our heart goes out to all the admins today. "This incident shows how dependent organizations are on a single ecosystem. Especially in critical infrastructure, monopolies are increasing the risk of stalling businesses globally if an incident occurs. "When everything is hanging on a single vendor, companies can't switch providers quickly to get back up and running, or have a second setup as backup, or pull the plug when under attack and keep working air-gapped." Similarly, Civo CEO Mark Boost noted that IT whoopsies were a way of life. "Every technology provider will experience failures," he said. "The real concern isn't that Microsoft has suffered an outage. It's that we've allowed so much of our critical infrastructure to become concentrated in the hands of so few companies, creating enormous single points of failure." Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, also commented: "The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK's digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services." This week, Microsoft warned users to treat its unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 as " permanently vulnerable ." Moving to Exchange Online brings its own dependencies, however. Beyond any compensation claims, Microsoft may face awkward conversations about those dependencies when contracts come up for renewal. And there are alternatives. Although perhaps not so extreme as the measures overheard by one vulture in a German shared workspace: "Germany's love of the fax machine – we are finally getti

item.title: Robinhood’s Crypto Trading Volume Falls 48% in October as Event Contracts More Than Double
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Robinhood’s Crypto Trading Volume Falls 48% in October as Event Contracts More Than Double Crypto trading on Robinhood fell by almost half from a year ago in October, the company said Thursday , as customers traded $17 billion of digital assets while their bets on event contracts more than doubled. The $17 billion figure was down 21% from September and 48% from October 2025, when crypto notional volume reached $32.5 billion. It covers both the flagship Robinhood app and Bitstamp, the crypto exchange the company bought in 2025. Volume in the Robinhood app fell to $6.8 billion, down 24% from September and 51% from a year earlier. Bitstamp handled $10.2 billion, down 18% month over month and 45% year over year. Average daily crypto volume across both platforms came to $548 million, compared with $713 million in September and about $1.05 billion a year ago. Daily average crypto trades slipped to about 700,000 from 900,000 in September and 1.1 million in October 2025. Event contracts take off as crypto cools The contrast with Robinhood’s prediction markets business is stark. Customers traded 5.9 billion event contracts in October, up 5% from September and 136% from the 2.5 billion traded a year earlier. Average daily volume reached 190 million contracts. Robinhood counts crypto and prediction markets on the same 31-day calendar, since both trade every day, so the comparison is apples to apples. Event contracts let users bet on outcomes such as elections, sports and economic data, and October’s tally covered the final weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. That growth has drawn scrutiny in Washington. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee in January, plans to crack down on prediction markets and election betting platforms. The rest of Robinhood’s brokerage held up better than crypto. Equity notional volume rose 2% from a year earlier to $325 billion, and options contracts traded climbed 8% to 289 million. Margin balances reached $22.9 billion, up 39% year over year. Funded customers rose by about 130,000 in the month to 28.9 million, and net deposits came to $15.1 billion. Total platform assets slipped 3% from September to $383 billion but were up 12% from a year earlier. Robinhood did not say why crypto activity fell. The release, like all of the company’s monthly updates, is unaudited and preliminary. Retail pulls back as bitcoin slides The slump in Robinhood’s crypto numbers lines up with a broader retreat by retail traders. Bitcoin ended September near $83,500 and has slid since, falling below $70,000 early Friday for the first time since August as a hot inflation report raised bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Institutional demand has cooled alongside it. U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds posted a sixth straight day of net outflows on Thursday, and BlackRock’s IBIT, the largest of them, bled about $2 billion over nine sessions through Wednesday. item.title: Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload
item.description: Arm's Lorenzo Stoakes isn't quitting Linux kernel development, though he's stepping back from some of the patch-review work he used to handle. Stoakes is a principal software engineer at Arm and he's a busy chap. Aside from writing the forthcoming book The Linux Memory Manager , in his CV [PDF], he says: "I hold four maintainerships: memory mapping, memory mapping (locking), memory mapping (madvise) – essentially the entirety of the userland API to memory management – and the reverse mapping which connects physical to virtual memory." Even so, he plans to soon be doing a little less. Earlier this week he posted an email to the Linux kernel mailing list to say that he was planning to drop some of his workload. He explained: "Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain. […] Apologies for doing this, but given the current trends I'd like to do something to make my inbox a little more manageable." As it happens, this came just the day after the Paramount Penguin himself said that he saw signs that the AI patch tide was "starting to turn." Stoakes told The Register : "I am retaining my maintainerships and have no plans on giving those up, I just want my inbox to be less horrendous. "And yeah, AI is part of the reason; in general, it's gone from 'once a week' to 'daily' to 'half of what I see in review'. "But the AI wave is hitting [memory management] across the board, really." He added: "I have a habit of burning myself out over weekends and evenings – you can see my involvement on a thread talking about that here - which gives you a sense of my views if you read back through that thread." At the Open Source Summit last month, the Reg FOSS desk joined the "Ask the Expert" session with Greg Kroah-Hartman , and he too expressed worrying sentiments: "The onslaught of the LLM-generated patches… we don't have enough people to review them all… We need more reviewers. We don't have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years." Kroah-Hartman also said: "I want to go down to two Long Term Support releases – four, maximum. Six is too many. We're too busy. We don't have the manpower. It’s crazy." On Red Hat's model of offering 10 years of support for products with a given version of the kernel: "Debian does it right. Debian and Yocto run the world. I've argued for years that the RHEL and SLES model is broken. That's why I don't work for SUSE any more." ®

item.title: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
item.description: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point. It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever. Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn't starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, "they will be squeezed to death," he wrote. Read full article Comments

item.title: I saw Saturn’s rings in seconds with the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian telescope — full review
item.description: null Saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it. The planet was at its biggest and brightest of the year, the seeing was good and its famous rings were visibly opening up after appearing edge-on from Earth in recent years. It was an obvious target for a new telescope. Finding it took seconds. After selecting Saturn in Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app, I followed the on-screen arrows as I moved the telescope across the sky. As I got closer, the app zoomed in until a bullseye turned green. I looked through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, then swapped to the 10mm to see a pale yellow Saturn at 75x magnification, with its rings sharply defined and its giant moon Titan visible in orbit. At 25 lbs (11.33 kg), the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian is a relative heavyweight. Jamie Carter The supplied 25mm and 10mm Kellner eyepieces provide 30x and 75x magnification, respectively, but are obvious candidates for future upgrades. Jamie Carter The StarSense Explorer smartphone dock uses a small mirror. Jamie Carter It was a stunning view, and exactly the kind of experience a beginner needs from a first telescope. There was no frustration and no wondering whether I was looking in the right place. StarSense took me straight there — but, crucially, I moved the telescope myself. I’ve always liked that combination of hand-holding and DIY observing that Celestron’s StarSense tech gives you. I’m less convinced by the tabletop telescope it’s attached to. Although this $599 RRP (£379) model is significantly smaller than the Celestron StarSense Explorer 8-inch Dobsonian telescope I’ve previously reviewed, it still weighs 25 lbs (11.33 kg). You need to place it on something sturdy before you can use it comfortably. After living with it in my backyard, I’m not convinced the tabletop format is the advantage it initially appears to be. An iPhone 16 Pro Max fitted securely into the StarSense Explorer smartphone dock during testing. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) What StarSense Explorer does well The Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian comes with a red dot finder for manual navigation. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) I’ve used Celestron’s StarSense Explorer system on a variety of telescopes and have always been impressed by how easy this type of smartphone navigation is to use. The technology works just as well here and, for me, it remains one of the best ways of making a traditional optical telescope accessible to a complete beginner. This isn’t a computerized GoTo telescope. There are no motors to slew across the sky automatically and no tracking system to keep an object centered. Instead, a smartphone sits in a dock attached to the telescope, and its camera looks at the sky via a small mirror. item.title: Astronaut Suni Williams rides through NYC as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade | Space photo of the day for Nov. 13, 2026
item.description: null NASA astronaut Suni Williams rides through New York City as the Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: Photo by Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images) New Yorkers got a space-y surprise on Wednesday (Nov. 11): Retired NASA astronaut and U.S. Navy Captain Sunita "Suni" Williams rolled down 5th Avenue in the back of a classic convertible wrapped in patriotic decals as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade. What is it? On Wednesday, New York City's 107th annual Veterans Day Parade made its way through Manhattan to the cheers and respectful nods of thousands of onlookers. The parade is an annual tradition on the holiday, which honors veterans of the U.S. armed forces. As part of the parade, veterans, active-duty soldiers, firefighters, marching bands, youth cadets and more march through the city and honor those who have served and sacrificed in the U.S. military. This year, the parade featured Suni Williams as its grand marshal. "I’m proud to join New Yorkers and Americans from around the country in honoring the service, sacrifice, and commitment of veterans from every generation," she said during the event. Why is it incredible? Williams was selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1998 and retired from it in December 2025 . She spent 608 days in space during her astronaut career, the second-most by an American astronaut behind Peggy Whitson , who racked up 695. Williams also had an extensive career in the U.S. Navy. She began as an ensign in 1987 before serving in a number of different roles. For example, she was a diving officer and a naval aviator and also provided helicopter combat support during Operation Desert Shield and Operation Provide Comfort. She further served as a squadron safety officer and finally as a captain, a rank she achieved in 2017. During this time, Williams supported relief efforts following Hurricane Andrew, trained within the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School and gained a wealth of further experience flying as a military pilot. Williams is part of a longstanding tradition of astronauts serving in the U.S. military. From test pilots to naval officers and more, there's a strong link between the U.S. armed forces and NASA's astronaut program.

item.title: Screenless GPS: Slate Auto says, "Remember the road atlas"
item.description: Whether it's nostalgia or a sense that technology has gotten a bit too pervasive, there’s no denying that Slate Auto appears to be tuned into the particular moment. The startup has a simple pitch : an affordable electric truck with just the basics , leaving owners to DIY and BYOD for everything else, all for a sub-$25,000 starting price. Among the things Slate does without is an embedded infotainment system. The small digital display on the dashboard that shows your speed and range is also where the backup camera appears if you engage reverse, and there are two USB-C ports that provide power but not connectivity, and that’s that. But there is a solution to getting lost, and it's called “Screenless GPS.” Even though we don’t have a Slate truck to test it with, the OEM sent us a unit to review. That’s right, it’s a good old spiral-bound road atlas! “We believe you should use the devices you know and love,” Slate says, and it reckons that maps worked just fine for past generations, so they should still work now. item.title: Most affairs don't matter except to the people involved. Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen's blunder will rock the world
item.description: It's a story as old as time. Billionaire nerd boy meets girl. Girl is later suspected of being a spy. News at 11. Oh, and it's also been reported that he was having an affair with one of his direct-report employees. When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a "romantic" blunder, he doesn't do it halfway. The boss of the world's most valuable company – well, it was until recently, anyway – publicly resigned yesterday, November 12, as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately. We don't know if he jumped or if he was pushed. He left after admitting to having an affair. Although he never named an affair partner, one of the affairs was reported to be with Alice Huang, AKA Huang Le. She's head of the Chinese company Megaspeed, which was an Nvidia partner. Megaspeed is accused of being a front for China's government that was used to transfer Nvidia chips to China, although this hasn't been proven. Some US officials also suspect [PDF] she's working for Chinese intelligence, although the DoJ said it hasn't yet reached a conclusion about this. The final nail in Jensen's coffin came when The New York Times reported he had also allegedly had an affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Jeeze, guy! In the aftermath, Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, was appointed interim CEO. She won't, I suspect, be in the job for long. CFOs are not CEOs. The jobs aren't remotely the same. In most companies, Huang would be replaced by the COO. That can't happen here. Nvidia doesn't have a COO. Both inside and outside of Nvidia, Huang is seen as Nvidia, and Nvidia as Huang. These days, billionaire CEOs are perceived as God-kings who know all and rule all. Much more often than not, that's BS. That isn't the case with Nvidia. Huang co-founded Nvidia on April 5, 1993. He was appointed CEO on day one, and he never left the job. At first, the company staggered forward. When it released the GeForce 256 in 1999 , which it marketed as the first GPU, it started on its path to becoming the chip manufacturer of choice for PC gamers. It still is today. That's a great niche, but it doesn't make a company a trillion-dollar business. No, the path to that dizzying height came when, in 2006, Nvidia unveiled CUDA . This programming architecture opened its GPUs' parallel-processing capabilities to scientific and other non-graphics workloads. From there, CUDA would become the foundation for most high-performance and AI computing. Huang was at the center of it all. He still was until now. At KubeCon North America , the trade show for Kubernetes, used in well over half of all AI projects, I spoke to many Nvidia employees. There were two things they all mentioned. First, they were in a state of shock. Maybe the top brass and government officials both in China and the US knew Huang was fooling with fire; the developer rank-and-file folks I spoke to hadn't had a clue. The second was that every month, Huang held an all-hands meeting where, instead of a per-forma corporate pep rally, h

item.title: President Trump Taps Two Democrats in Bipartisan Slate of SEC and CFTC Nominees as Both Agencies Run Short-Handed
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine President Trump Taps Two Democrats in Bipartisan Slate of SEC and CFTC Nominees as Both Agencies Run Short-Handed President Donald Trump sent the Senate four nominees for the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission on Thursday, his first picks for either agency in about a year and the first Democrats he has put forward for them. Former CFTC Commissioner Kristin Johnson, a Democrat, and Republican Steven Levine were nominated to the SEC. Republican Nathan Anonick and Democrat Matthew Rowland were nominated to the CFTC, Bloomberg Law reported. Each nominee needs Senate confirmation. The Senate Banking Committee will handle the SEC picks, while the Senate Agriculture Committee will take up the CFTC pair before any vote by the full chamber. Who the nominees are Levine was tapped for the SEC seat left by Hester Peirce, whose term expired, for a term running through June 5, 2030. He most recently served as general counsel and a senior adviser at the White House Council of Economic Advisers and previously worked at the SEC as counsel and deputy chief of staff to Commissioner Mark Uyeda. Peirce led the SEC’s Crypto Task Force and was one of the agency’s most vocal supporters of clearer crypto rules. Johnson would take the seat formerly held by Democrat Caroline Crenshaw, for a term ending June 5, 2029. She served as a CFTC commissioner until 2025 and is a former law school professor. During her time at the CFTC, she spoke often about digital assets, including custody and decentralized finance. Both CFTC nominees come from the Senate Agriculture Committee, which oversees the derivatives regulator. Anonick is legislative counsel to Chairman John Boozman and was a lead negotiator on the committee’s portion of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. He was nominated to the seat once held by former Chairman Rostin Behnam, for a term ending June 19, 2031. Rowland is a CFTC attorney detailed to the committee who also worked on the Clarity Act and the committee’s 2024 crypto bill. He previously served on Johnson’s staff at the CFTC, according to his LinkedIn profile. He would fill the remainder of former Commissioner Summer Mersinger’s term, which expires April 13, 2028. Both agencies can seat up to five commissioners, with no more than three from one party. The SEC currently has two, Chairman Paul Atkins and Commissioner Mark Uyeda. Chairman Mike Selig is the CFTC’s only sitting commissioner. Lame-duck timing and a Democratic Senate The timing puts the nominees in front of a Senate in its lame-duck session, weeks after Democrats swept both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, one of crypto’s sharpest critics, is expected to chair the Banking Committee when the new Congress is seated in January. The pairing of Democrats with Republicans could matter for confirmation. After the election, TD Cowen’s Jaret Seiberg told clients he did not expect Democrats to confirm Trump nominees
